summary: Defines an experimental scheme for Internet encapsulation, in which IP datagrams get an extra header and are routed between encapsulators and decapsulators along flows. The authors were Woodburn and Mills. It is an Experimental protocol, version 1.

plainLanguage.summary:
This RFC describes how to carry a datagram through a part of the network that does not normally route it, by wrapping it in a second IP header.

The sender does not have to know the path. An intermediate machine decides which tunnel the datagram belongs to by matching its header against a table, and a number in the tunnel header tells the far end where to send it next.

what is a flow id in encapsulation
what is an ip encapsulation protocol
subtitle: How a datagram is carried across an encapsulation space in a tunnel, without the sender knowing the path.

tldr.problem: Researchers needed a way to tunnel between networks, to bypass routing failures, avoid broken gateways or routing domains, or set up deterministic paths, and the existing options all required the source to know the topology.
tldr.mechanism: A new IP encapsulation protocol puts an IP header for a separate encapsulation space, plus a small protocol header carrying a Flow ID, in front of the original datagram. An Encapsulator chooses the flow by matching the original header against a table of masks.
tldr.outcome: The encapsulation is transparent to everything in the user space except the Encapsulator. The document is Experimental and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 1241 is an Experimental document from July 1991 and has not been obsoleted. It describes version 1 of an Internet encapsulation protocol, and it notes that until then there had been no standard for an encapsulation protocol.

sections.title: The Terms the Protocol Uses
sections.content:
The protocol is built on a small set of defined terms. The Clear Datagram is the unmodified IP datagram in the User Space before encapsulation, and the Clear Header is the header portion of that datagram, which includes the IP header and possibly part or all of the next layer protocol header, such as the TCP header. The Encapsulated Datagram is the datagram consisting of a Clear Datagram with an Encapsulation Header prepended, and the Encapsulation Header is that prepended header, which consists of an IP header followed by an Encapsulation Protocol Header, the protocol-specific part of it. Encapsulation is the process of mapping a Clear Datagram to the Encapsulation Space, prepending the header and routing the result, and Decapsulation is the stripping of the header and forwarding of the Clear Datagram by the Decapsulator.

An Encapsulator is the entity responsible for mapping a given User Space datagram to the Encapsulation Space, encapsulating it, and forwarding the Encapsulated Datagram to a Decapsulator; it may be a host or a gateway. A Decapsulator receives an Encapsulated Datagram, decapsulates it and delivers it to the destination User Space, either directly or via further encapsulation; it may also be a host or a gateway.

A User Space is the address and routing space within which the users reside, providing reachability between all address pairs within it. A User Address is the address or identifier uniquely identifying an entity within a User Space. An Encapsulation Space is the address and routing space within which the Encapsulators and Decapsulators reside, and routing within it is accomplished via Flows. A Flow, also called a tunnel, is the end-to-end path in the Encapsulation Space over which Encapsulated Datagrams travel; there may be several Encapsulator and Decapsulator pairs along a given flow, and a flow does not denote what user space gateways are traversed along the path. A Flow ID is a 32-bit identifier which uniquely distinguishes a flow in a given Encapsulator or Decapsulator; flow IDs are specific to a single entity and are not global quantities. A Mapping Function maps a Clear Header to a particular flow, and all encapsulators along a given flow are required to map a given Clear Header to the same flow. A Source Route is a complete end-to-end route computed at the source which enumerates the transit gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol separates the network the user is in from the network the tunnel runs in. The datagram the user sends is called the clear datagram; the one that travels in the tunnel is the encapsulated datagram.

sections.title: What Encapsulation Is For
sections.content:
For several years researchers in the Internet community had needed a means of tunneling between networks. A tunnel is essentially a source route that circumvents conventional routing mechanisms. Tunnels provide the means to bypass routing failures, avoid broken gateways and routing domains, or establish deterministic paths for experimentation.

There were several means of accomplishing tunneling. In the past it had been done through source routing options in the IP header, which allow gateways along a path to be enumerated. The disadvantage is that source routing requires the source to know something about the networks traversed to reach the destination, and to modify outgoing packets to reflect the source route; current routing implementations generally do not support source routes in their routing tables as a means of reaching an IP address, nor do current routing protocols.

Another means would be to develop a new IP option, in a separate IP header that could be prepended to an IP datagram, indicating information about the original datagram. That has the disadvantage of significantly modifying existing IP implementations to handle a new IP option, and it is less flexible in permitting the tunneling of other protocols, such as ISO protocols, through an IP environment. An even less palatable alternative would be to replace IP with a new networking protocol, or a new version of IP with tunneling built in as part of its functionality.

The final alternative is what this RFC takes: a new IP encapsulation protocol that uses the current IP header format. By using encapsulation, a destination can be reached transparently without the source having to know topology specifics, and virtual networks can be created by tying otherwise unconnected machines together with flows through an encapsulation space. Up until then there had been no standard for an encapsulation protocol, and this RFC provides a means of performing encapsulation in the Internet environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunneling lets two machines talk over a path that the ordinary routing does not know about. The earlier ways of doing this all needed changes to IP or to the routing tables; this one only adds a header.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture is based on two entities, an Encapsulator and a Decapsulator, and the associated spaces. Encapsulation Spaces do not overlap, so the address of any Encapsulator or Decapsulator is unique across them, and User Spaces do not overlap either, so a given user address is unique in all User Spaces.

Encapsulators and Decapsulators have addresses in the User Spaces to which they belong, as well as addresses in the Encapsulation Spaces to which they belong. An Encapsulator receives a Clear Datagram from its User Space and, after determining that encapsulation should be used, performs a mapping function which translates the user space information in the Clear Header into an Encapsulation Header. That header is prepended to the Clear Datagram to form the Encapsulated Datagram. The encapsulation process is desirable if it is transparent to entities in the User Space: only the Encapsulator needs to know that encapsulation is occurring.

The Encapsulator forwards the datagram to a Decapsulator whose identity is determined at the time of encapsulation. The Decapsulator removes the Encapsulation Header and treats the Clear Datagram as if it had been received locally. The requirement on the address of the Decapsulator is that it be reachable from the Encapsulator's Encapsulation Space address.

Using the encapsulation protocol requires a modification to IP forwarding, so that the IP module can pass Clear Datagrams to the encapsulation protocol. A suggested means is to add a flag to a route in the routing table structures, telling the forwarding function to use encapsulation; the default route could also be set to use encapsulation. The forwarding mechanism would then examine its routing tables to match the IP destination to a specific route, check whether encapsulation should be used, and if so send the datagram to encapsulation for forwarding. At the last Decapsulator on a flow, decapsulated datagrams are injected into the output portion of IP, and the source address in the Clear Header must not change: it must remain the address of the source in the source User Space and not be overwritten with that of the Decapsulator. Because of the modification to the routing table, it also becomes possible to specify a virtual interface whose sole purpose is encapsulation, which allows a virtual network to be constructed that overlays the actual routing topology.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two separate address spaces: the one the user's own network uses, and the one the tunnel runs in. A machine at the entrance of the tunnel wraps the datagram for the tunnel space; a machine at the far end unwraps it and puts it back into the user's space.

sections.title: Generating the Encapsulation Header
sections.content:
The contents of the Encapsulation Header are produced by a mapping function from the Clear Header. In the first part of that function the Clear Header is matched with stored headers and masks to determine a Flow ID, which is essentially a mask-and-match table lookup where the table holds three entries: a Clear Header, a header mask and a corresponding Flow ID. The mask allows a range of source and destination addresses to map to a given flow, and other fields such as the IP TOS bits or even the TCP source or destination port addresses could also be used to discriminate between flows. This flexibility allows many possibilities: not only can a given network be associated with a particular flow, but even a particular TCP protocol or connection could be distinguished from another. How the lookup table is built and maintained is not part of this protocol; it is assumed to be managed by some higher layer entity, and it would be sufficient to configure the tables from ASCII text files.

The Flow IDs are managed at a higher layer as well. The RFC points to the Setup protocol of the Inter-Domain Policy Sensitive Routing Protocol as an example, and notes that the upper layer protocol would be responsible for maintaining information not carried in the encapsulation protocol, such as the type of data being encapsulated, currently only IP, and the type of authentication used if any.

The Flow ID that results from the mapping is a 32-bit quantity identifying the flow as seen by the Encapsulator. If a datagram must be encapsulated and decapsulated several times to reach the destination, the Flow ID may be different at each Encapsulator but need not be. It acts as an index into a table of Encapsulation Header information used to build the header. Making the Flow ID local to the Encapsulator is due to the difficulty of choosing and maintaining globally unique identifiers. The intermediate step of using a Flow ID is entirely optional: the important requirement is that all Encapsulators along a flow map the same Clear Header to the same flow, which could be identified by different identifiers along the way.

The information needed to build the Encapsulation Header is the Flow ID relative to the current Encapsulator, the IP address of the Decapsulator in the Encapsulation Space, the Flow ID for the flow as seen by the Decapsulator if any, the previous Encapsulator's address if this is not the first Encapsulator along the flow, for error reporting, and the previous Encapsulator's Flow ID. The two pieces of information that must be determined at the time of encapsulation for the Encapsulation Protocol Header are the protocol being encapsulated and the Flow ID to send to the Decapsulator.

The generation of the IP header is more complicated, because each field in the Clear Header could relate to the new IP header in one of two ways: Copy, meaning the existing field is copied across, or Ignore, meaning the field may or may not have existed in the Clear Header but does not apply to the new IP header. Most fields in the Clear Header are simply ignored: fields such as the Header Length in the Clear Header have no effect on the Header Length of the new IP header. The Quality of Service bits should be copied, in keeping with the transparency principle that if the User Space was providing a given service, the Encapsulation Space must provide the same service. The More Fragments bit and Fragment Offset should not be copied, since the datagram being built is a complete datagram regardless of the status of the encapsulated datagram; if the completed datagram is too large for the interface it will be fragmented by the normal IP fragmentation mechanism. The Don't Fragment bit should not be copied either, because the transparency principle would again be violated; it should be up to the Encapsulator to decide whether fragmentation is allowed across the Encapsulation Space, and if the DF bit is used then an ICMP message would be returned if the Encapsulated Datagram required fragmentation across the Encapsulation Space.

For the TTL the easiest thing to do is to ignore the TTL from the Clear Header, since copying it could mean the packet life is prematurely exceeded during transit in the Encapsulation Space. The TTL of the Clear Header is decremented before encapsulation by the IP forwarding function, so there is no chance of a packet looping forever if the links of a flow form a loop. The protocol field of the new IP header should carry the protocol number of the encapsulation protocol, the source address becomes the IP address of the Encapsulator in the Encapsulation Domain, and the destination address becomes the IP address of the Decapsulator as found in the encapsulation table. IP options are generally not copied because most do not make sense in the context of the Encapsulation Space, and the security option is probably the one that should be copied, for the same reason the QoS and precedence fields are copied.

The protocol header itself is eight octets long. The first octet holds the version number of the encapsulation protocol in four bits, and the version described by this document is 1, and the header length in octets in the other four bits. The second octet holds the message type in four bits and the reason code in the other four bits: a data message has a message type of 1 and an error message has a message type of 2, the reason code is unused in a data message and must be 0, and in an error message it holds the reason code, of which 1 is Unknown Flow ID and 2 is ICMP returned. The next two octets carry a 16-bit one's complement checksum for the header, set to zero while the checksum is calculated and filled in with the result before the data message is sent. The last four octets carry the 32-bit Flow ID as seen by the Encapsulator or Decapsulator the message is being sent to; in an Unknown Flow ID error, the Flow ID causing the error is used. For data messages the protocol header is followed by the Clear Datagram, and for error messages it is followed by the ICMP message being forwarded along a flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapping decision is a table lookup: the original header is matched against a mask, and the match gives a number identifying the tunnel. The new IP header is mostly built fresh, but the type-of-service bits and the security option are carried across so the service the user gets does not change.

sections.title: Decapsulation
sections.content:
In the ideal situation a Decapsulator receives an Encapsulated Datagram, strips off the Encapsulation Header and sends the Clear Datagram back into IP so that it is forwarded from that point. However, if the Clear Datagram has not reached the destination User Space, it must again be encapsulated to move it closer to the destination User Space. In that case the Decapsulator becomes an Encapsulator and performs the same calculation to generate the next Encapsulation Header as the previous Encapsulator did. To make this more efficient, the use of Flow IDs has been incorporated into the protocol.

When Flow IDs are used, the Flow ID received in the Encapsulation Header corresponds to a stored Flow ID in the Decapsulator, and the Decapsulator has the option of bypassing the mask and match operation on the Clear Header. The received Flow ID can be used to point directly into the local tables for the construction of the next Encapsulation Header. If the Flow ID is unknown, an error message is sent back to the previous Encapsulator and a signal is sent to the upper layer entity managing the encapsulation tables.

Because the normal IP forwarding mechanism is bypassed when Flow IDs are used, certain mechanisms normally handled by IP must be taken care of by the Decapsulator. The Decapsulator must decrement the TTL before the next encapsulation occurs, and if a Time Exceeded error occurs, an ICMP message is sent to the source indicated in the Clear Header.
sections.plainLanguage: At each end of the tunnel the number in the header says which tunnel it is. If the far end does not know that number it reports it back, and if a packet expires the far end sends the error to the original sender rather than to the tunnel.

sections.title: Error Messages, Fragmentation and Forwarding
sections.content:
There are two kinds of error message built into the encapsulation protocol. The first reports unknown flow identifiers seen by a Decapsulator: the Decapsulator notifies the previous Encapsulator that the flow was not known, so that the problem may be reported to the layer responsible for programming the flow tables. The second is for forwarding ICMP messages. If an Encapsulator receives an ICMP message regarding a given flow, the message should be forwarded backwards along the flow to the source Encapsulator. The ICMP message will contain the Flow ID of the message which caused the error, and this Flow ID must be translated to the Flow ID relative to the Encapsulator the error message is sent to. If an error occurs while sending any error message, no further error messages are generated.

The handling of ICMP messages is called the most controversial aspect of encapsulation. Because the Encapsulation Header contains the source address of the Encapsulator in the Encapsulation Space, ICMP messages which occur within the Encapsulation Space are sent back to the Encapsulator. The original source of the Clear Datagram knows nothing about the Encapsulation Space, so forwarding an ICMP message on to it does not make sense, and ICMP messages are not supposed to beget ICMP messages; yet not sending the original source something may break some important mechanisms. There is also the problem of possibly not having enough information to send anything at all back: an ICMP message returns the header of the offending message and the first eight octets of the data after it, which for the encapsulation protocol means the IP portion of the Encapsulation Header, the first eight octets of the Encapsulation Protocol Header and nothing else, so the contents of the Clear Datagram are completely lost and the Encapsulator would have to reconstruct the Clear Header, which is essentially impossible to do exactly. The Flow ID has been assumed to be a unique one-way mapping from a Clear Header, with no guarantee that it could be used to map back.

The RFC divides the ICMP messages into three categories. The first are those not applicable in the context of encapsulation: Echo and Echo Reply, and Timestamp and Timestamp Reply. The second concern mechanisms local to the encapsulation domain and would not make sense to the original source, such as Parameter Problem, Redirect, Destination Unreachable and Time Exceeded; for these the datagram is simply lost, since IP is not meant to be a reliable protocol. The third is the ICMP Source Quench message, for which the only possible mechanism available to the Encapsulator is to set a flag for the offending Flow ID so that subsequent messages mapping that flow cause a source quench to be generated back to the original source before the datagram is encapsulated.

One immediate concern with encapsulation is restrictions based on MTU size. The source of a Clear Datagram generates packets consistent with the MTU of the interface over which the datagram is transmitted, and if these reach an Encapsulator and are encapsulated they may be fragmented if they are larger than the MTU of the Encapsulator, even though the physical interfaces of the source and the Encapsulator may have the same MTU. Because a new header is prepended by the encapsulation process, the likelihood of fragmentation increases, and if the Encapsulator disallows fragmentation through the Encapsulation Space it must send an ICMP message back to the source, which means the effective MTU of the interface in the encapsulation space is smaller than the physical MTU of the interface. Fragmentation by intermediate user space gateways introduces another problem, because fragmentation occurs at the IP level and, if TCP is in use, the TCP header is contained in the first fragment but not the following ones, so discrimination of the Clear Header for a given flow can only be done on the IP header portion.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need care. A wrapped datagram is bigger than the original, so it may have to be split on the way. And the wrapping changes what a broken path reports back, so the RFC works out which ICMP messages should cross the tunnel and which should not.

fields.name: Vers
fields.desc: The version of the encapsulation protocol. This document describes version 1.

fields.name: HL
fields.desc: The header length of the Encapsulation Protocol Header in octets.

fields.name: MT
fields.desc: The message type: 1 for a data message, 2 for an error message.

fields.name: RC
fields.desc: The reason code. Unused in a data message, where it must be 0. In an error message, 1 is Unknown Flow ID and 2 is ICMP returned.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: A one's complement checksum for the Encapsulation Protocol Header, set to zero while calculating.

fields.name: Flow ID
fields.desc: The flow as seen by the Encapsulator or Decapsulator the message is sent to.

messages.note: The datagram arrives with the addresses of its own user space.

messages.label: Encapsulated Datagram
messages.note: An IP header for the encapsulation space and the Encapsulation Protocol Header are prepended, and the flow is chosen by matching the Clear Header.

messages.label: Clear Datagram
messages.note: The Decapsulator strips the header and forwards the datagram locally, keeping the original source address.
